periods.activity_title: Who Are Our Elderly? — Pre-Reading Activation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.97): graphic organiser — caring for the elderly, group discussion

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter title and invites students to share what they know about elderly relatives at home or in their neighbourhood. A brief whole-class exchange surfaces lived experiences before any text is opened.

Students individually complete the Reflect and Respond graphic organiser — four prompts on why we care for the elderly, problems they face, likely causes, and how we can help. Teacher circulates and prompts shy students with a quiet question or a nod.
Pairs share their organiser responses; teacher opens a class discussion, collecting ideas on the board under the four headings. Students note one idea they had not thought of before.

Teacher closes by naming the story's central character, Grandpa, and asking students to predict one tension that might arise between him and his city-dwelling family — a question held open for the reading ahead.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the chapter's entry point. The discussion draws on personal experience, so any student can contribute regardless of reading ability. Remind students that every observation is valid — Grandpa's story will surprise many of their assumptions about elderly people being passive or forgetful.
materials: Textbook p.97 (Reflect and Respond graphic organiser)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.98): vocabulary self-assessment table — six key story words

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the six words — frail, shuddered, poky, forbid, pottering, winced — on the board and reads each aloud with natural stress. Students echo the pronunciation and make a first guess at meaning from sound alone.

Students work individually on the four-column vocabulary table for all six words: ticking whether they have not heard the word, have heard it but are unsure, know it partially, or can write a meaning. Teacher circulates and resists giving answers — the ambiguity is part of the exercise.

Pairs compare their tables and negotiate the two or three words they disagree on; they then consult a dictionary to settle on meanings and write these in the fourth column. Teacher draws attention to how context clues might help — e.g. 'poky little flat' gives a spatial sense.
Quick whole-class share: teacher asks which word surprised students most and invites a sentence using it in a city-flat or family context.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have heard a word passively often overestimate their understanding; the four-column table makes this honest without embarrassment. The words frail and poky are particularly loaded in the story's argument about how Grandpa is perceived versus how he sees himself — flag this without explaining it yet, letting the reading surface it.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.97): tradition or recipe from an elderly relative — personal share

time_bands.activity: Teacher gives a brief personal anecdote (one or two sentences) about a tradition or skill learned from an older relative, then asks two or three students to share their own — priming Task III's discussion in a quick, warm exchange.

Task III: a quick paired share on a tradition, story, or recipe passed down by an elderly relative, and what it means personally. Teacher invites one or two pairs to share with the class before moving to reading.

Shared reading of pp.97–102 (the opening of the story through the first section's close): teacher reads aloud with expression, pausing twice — once at the Vitamin-M wish and once at Grandpa's walking-out moment — for students to predict what happens next. Students follow in their textbooks.
Brief open response: teacher asks students what one word they would use to describe Grandpa at this point and why — a quick verbal check of first impressions.

periods.teacher_notes: Read the opening paragraph — Vidya's Vitamin-M wish — with a slightly comic, exasperated tone so students catch that she does not know Grandpa can hear her; this is a crucial dramatic irony the comprehension questions will return to. The read-aloud is unhurried; do not rush to cover pages at the expense of tone and student attention.

periods.activity_title: Check Your Understanding — Section I Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.102): four questions on Grandpa's city dislike, Vidya's fears, Ravi's sympathy, and Ravi's dilemma

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the final image from the read-aloud — Grandpa striding out with his mahogany stick and yellow cap — and asks students to hold that image in mind as they approach the comprehension questions about what brought him to the city.

Students write individual responses to all four Check Your Understanding questions (p.102): why Grandpa dislikes city life, why Vidya fears him going out, whether Ravi sides with Grandpa, and whether Ravi can keep his promise. Teacher circulates and prompts students to cite the text.

Teacher leads a whole-class discussion of the four questions, building a 'character motive' map on the board — three columns for Grandpa, Vidya, and Ravi, each row showing what each character wants and fears. Students add details from their written answers.

Teacher poses a closing inference question: 'Who is actually more aware of the situation — Grandpa or Vidya?' Students give a one-sentence verdict and hold it as a reading purpose for the story's second section.

periods.teacher_notes: The third question — whether Ravi sides with Grandpa — invites genuine disagreement; Ravi's silence and his body language in the text suggest empathy without open defiance. Push students to distinguish what a character says from what the text implies about their feelings. The incident of Grandpa lying outside all night is the factual reason for Vidya's fear — students should be precise about this rather than offering a vague answer about 'old age'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the story's situation — Grandpa has just walked out, Ravi is left behind — asking a student to describe Ravi's predicament in one sentence before the reading begins.

Shared reading of pp.102–106 (the comedy-of-errors surveillance sequence): teacher reads Grandpa's sections with confidence and Ravi's sections with a hushed, anxious tone, pausing after each misadventure (the elephant bush, the banyan tree vendors, the Ladies' Hairdressing Salon) to let students laugh and predict the next disaster. Students follow in their textbooks.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks: the funniest moment so far and why it works as comedy — a quick personal response that feeds the critical reflection work ahead.

periods.teacher_notes: The comic set-pieces (elephant bush, shrieking salon women, vendor confusion) work best with varying vocal energy — read Ravi's humiliations with a small, mortified tone and Grandpa's oblivious strides with cheerful confidence. Students who find the story funny are already doing analytical work; the 'why it works' sentence prepares them for later questions about the author's craft.

periods.activity_title: Flow Chart and Inference — Section II Comprehension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.106): seven-blank flow chart of Grandpa's day out
Check Your Understanding (p.107): three inference questions — Grandpa safe?, Ravi's feelings, mother knowing

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the seven-box flow chart frame on the board and asks students what information they will need to complete it — a quick scanning preview before they write.

Students complete the seven-blank flow chart (p.106) individually, tracking Grandpa's route: park, fruit stall, tea stall, barber shop, bus stop. Teacher circulates, nudging students to check specific pages for detail rather than guessing.

Teacher builds the correct flow chart on the board collaboratively — asking a different student for each blank — then moves to the three inference questions (p.107): Was Grandpa lost? How does Ravi feel on seeing him safe? Will Vidya find out?

Whole-class discussion of the three inference questions; teacher probes students on what textual evidence supports their prediction about whether Vidya will find out, opening a strand of dramatic irony that the story's ending will resolve.

periods.teacher_notes: The flow chart blank about Ravi being 'scolded by' two different parties (the mother in the park and the vendor women) sometimes confuses students — remind them to read the flow chart prompt carefully and to distinguish whose wrath falls on Ravi at each stop. The prediction question about Vidya finding out is deliberately open; accept any answer that is grounded in the text's logic, since the story's twist makes both 'yes' and 'no' partially right.

periods.activity_title: Reading Aloud — The Twist and Birthday Gifts (pp.107–109)

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to predict, in a sentence, how the story will end — will Grandpa be in trouble? Will Ravi be found out? A brief show of hands on each prediction makes the stakes visible before reading.

Shared reading of pp.107–109 (Grandpa's cool revelation, the birthday gifts, the Vitamin-M counter): teacher pauses after Grandpa's 'quiet morning' line for the class to appreciate the irony, then reads the gift-giving sequence at a warmer pace. Students follow in textbooks.
Students write two to three sentences in their notebooks: what surprised them about the ending and whether their prediction was right.

periods.teacher_notes: Grandpa's 'quiet morning' speech is the story's comic and emotional peak; read it with a controlled, deadpan calm so students feel the full effect of the reversal. The gift-giving tradition — Grandpa gives gifts on his own birthday — is a key character detail that disproves the assumption of failing memory; ensure students notice this before the critical reflection questions address it directly.

periods.activity_title: Section III Check and Character Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.109): three questions — Ravi's emotional reaction, birthday gift-giving significance, detective book meaning

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the question: 'What single moment in the story best shows Grandpa's character?' Students share briefly — a warm entry into analytical thinking before the written task.

Students write individual responses to all three Check Your Understanding questions (p.109): Ravi's emotional reaction, the significance of Grandpa's gift-giving tradition, and why Grandpa chose The Best Detective Stories for Ravi. Teacher circulates and asks students to push beyond 'Ravi was happy' toward what specific emotion the text implies.

Whole-class discussion: teacher builds a mini literary analysis — what do the three questions, taken together, reveal about Grandpa's intelligence and emotional intelligence? Students note one phrase from the story that demonstrates Grandpa's awareness.
Teacher names the Critical Reflection tasks ahead and previews the kind of thinking they demand — close reading of an extract plus analytical questions.

periods.teacher_notes: The third question — why a detective story? — is the story's most playful moment of meta-awareness; Grandpa's wink signals he knew all along. Students sometimes misread the gift as random; push them to see it as Grandpa's affectionate acknowledgement of Ravi's efforts. The emotional reaction question (Ravi's relief at seeing Grandpa safe) is evidence of real affection beneath their comic relationship — a theme the critical reflection will deepen.

periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection — Extract Analysis, Extracts 1 and 2

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.109–110): Extract 1 — five questions on Grandpa's nostalgia, small-town life, and his move to the city
Critical Reflection (p.110–111): Extract 2 — five questions on Grandpa's cool tone, Ravi's embarrassment, and the birthday confusion

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains what 'close reading of an extract' means at secondary level — not just comprehension but noticing tone, word choice, and the gap between what a character says and what they feel — then reads Extract 1 aloud.

Students work individually on all five Extract 1 questions (p.109–110): the emotion Grandpa displays, the reason he hated city life, why he came despite that hatred, the meaning of 'hear a leaf fall', and one advantage and one disadvantage of his small-town home. Teacher circulates and prompts students to justify choices with the extract's wording.
Teacher reads Extract 2 aloud with particular attention to the word 'coolly' and the word 'impatiently' — asking students to notice how tone is carried in a single adverb before they answer.

Students work individually on all five Extract 2 questions (p.110–111): Grandpa's tone, why Ravi is confused and embarrassed, why Vidya is impatient, whether Grandpa forgot the birthday (true/false), and why Grandpa says he did not know about Ravi's morning. Teacher circulates.
Brief pair check: each pair compares answers to the two True/False or MCQ items, then teacher gives the correct responses and a one-sentence explanation of each.

periods.teacher_notes: The MCQ asking students to distinguish 'nostalgic' from 'wistful' is deliberately subtle — both describe longing, but nostalgia is specifically for the past while wistfulness is more generally yearning; the text's detail about the mango tree and village sounds tips the balance toward 'nostalgic'. Extract 2's True/False statement ('Grandfather forgot that Ravi's birthday was three months ago') is FALSE — Grandpa knows perfectly well and is giving a gift on his own birthday; make sure students state their justification from the text.

periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection II — Character, Theme, and Debate

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection II (p.111): eight analytical questions — character traits, detective debate, ageism, who needs Vitamin-M

time_bands.activity: Teacher divides the eight Critical Reflection II questions into three clusters: memory and evidence (Q1), character traits (Q2), narrative questions (Q3–Q6), and thematic/personal response (Q7–Q8) — giving students a map before they begin.

Students work individually through all eight questions, starting with the two evidence-based ones (disproving Grandpa's 'failing memory'; two traits per character) before moving to the more open reflective ones. Teacher circulates, asking students to push past single-word answers for the trait questions.

Whole-class discussion led by the teacher: Q5 ('Ravi is a good detective' — one argument for, one against) is debated briefly as a class, with teacher modelling how to structure a balanced argument. Q7 ('who needs Vitamin-M?') draws personal responses that revisit the story's central irony.

Teacher closes by naming the story's themes explicitly — intergenerational dignity, autonomy, selective memory, quiet love — and asking students to match each theme to one specific moment in the story. This consolidates the analytical work done across the reading units.

periods.teacher_notes: Question 1 requires two concrete pieces of evidence against the 'failing memory' label — Grandpa's chess knowledge and his precise memory of his own birthday tradition are the strongest choices from the text. Students sometimes argue for both sides of Q5 by contradicting themselves; model a clean two-paragraph structure (for: he tracked Grandpa's route; against: he boarded the wrong bus) before they write. Question 8 on age-based discrimination is open to personal experience — accept any honest example and connect it back to the story's treatment of Grandpa.

periods.activity_title: Vocabulary in Motion — Movement and Sound Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.112): classify movement vs. sound words, then fill in Detective Shankar passage (ten blanks)

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.113): find synonyms for DILEMMA — QUANDARY and PREDICAMENT using letter prompts

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the twenty-word box aloud at pace — pottering, boomed, twirling, crouch, bustle, crawl, creeping, thudded, ducked, shrieks, zigzagging, whirr, evicted, briskly, sprinting, grunted, jumping, darted, trailing, snoring — and asks students to physically mime two or three as teacher names them.

Students classify all twenty words into the two columns — movement and sound — noting that some (like 'evicted') are narrative actions rather than physical sounds; teacher takes a show-of-hands vote on disputed cases and leads a short explanation.

Students fill in all ten blanks of the Detective Shankar passage using words from their completed columns. Teacher reads the passage aloud once before they write, so the register and pace of the detective story are clear.

Teacher reads the completed passage aloud with student-chosen answers inserted, asking the class to vote on any blank where two words are possible — building metalinguistic awareness of register and precision.

periods.teacher_notes: The word 'evicted' sits awkwardly between categories — it describes an action that occurs with noise (Ravi being ejected from the salon) and so some students will place it in sound; accept this and use the discussion to show how context determines category. The Detective Shankar passage is a playful mirror of Ravi's own surveillance comedy — point this out so students see the vocabulary exercise as connected to the story's texture.
materials: Textbook p.112 (Vocabulary and Structures in Context, Task I)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.113): six-word meaning table — craftily, dilemma, furious, boomed, humiliation, attire
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.113): match five emotion words to meanings — one meaning is extra

time_bands.activity: Teacher returns quickly to the homework word DILEMMA from the previous unit's homework, confirms its two synonyms (QUANDARY, PREDICAMENT), then pivots: 'DILEMMA appears in today's six-word table — we'll go deeper this time.'

Students complete the six-column meaning table (p.113) for craftily, dilemma, furious, boomed, humiliation, attire — filling in meaning, part of speech, synonym, and antonym. Teacher circulates and encourages dictionary use for antonyms specifically, which students find harder.

Students tackle the matching task (p.113): five emotion or expression words (embarrassed, countered, flushed, stricken, gleam) matched to six meanings, one meaning being extra. Teacher reminds students to use the story's scenes — Ravi's salon exit, Grandpa's cool speech — as context clues.

Teacher leads a collaborative check of the matching task, explaining the extra meaning (option ii, 'to be confused') and why none of the five words maps to it precisely — a miniature lesson in semantic discrimination.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate 'embarrassed' (felt uncomfortable about something) with 'flushed' (became red in the face); the story gives both in Ravi's salon scene — use it to show these are two distinct phenomena that happen to co-occur. The six-word table's 'boomed' is worth connecting to the sound-word column from the previous vocabulary unit, reinforcing domain vocabulary across exercises.
materials: Textbook p.113 (Vocabulary and Structures in Context, Tasks III and IV)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.114): underline prepositions in four phrases; fill six blanks with correct prepositions
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.114–116): sentence-type analysis and reported-speech transformation — Arvind–Priya conversation, six blanks

time_bands.activity: Students underline the prepositions in the four given phrases from the story (across, over, under, behind) and then fill in the six blanks of the contextualised passage choosing from the given options. Teacher works through the first blank together with the class to model the elimination strategy.

Teacher introduces the grammar note on interrogative sentences and direct versus indirect (reported) speech, using the five story dialogues as illustrations — asking students to identify the sentence type and whether intonation would rise or fall.

Students work through the four sentence-type multiple-choice questions (i–iv) on pp.114–115, then complete all six reported-speech blanks in the Arvind–Priya conversation (p.116). Teacher circulates and addresses the common error of retaining 'said that' but forgetting to shift tense.

Collaborative board check: teacher writes three of the six reported-speech answers and asks volunteers to explain the tense shift applied in each — making the rule visible in the correction rather than just giving answers.

periods.teacher_notes: Reported-speech tense backshift (present→past, will→would, can→could) is the central grammatical challenge; students often drop the tense shift when the reporting verb is 'said'. Use the Grandpa–Ravi dialogues from the story to create a second oral example if students need reinforcement — e.g. transforming Grandpa's 'I had a quiet morning' into reported form makes the grammar personally relevant.
materials: Textbook pp.114–116 (Vocabulary and Structures in Context, Tasks V and VI)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.116–117): meditation podcast — complete five sentence-completion blanks with exact words heard

time_bands.activity: Teacher previews the five incomplete sentences (p.116–117) so students know what to listen for, then frames the listening task: 'You are completing each blank with no more than three exact words from what you hear — precision matters, not paraphrase.'

Teacher reads the meditation podcast transcript aloud at a steady pace (or plays the audio if available), while students listen and note key words. Students do not write in blanks yet — this first pass is for global understanding.
Teacher reads (or plays) the podcast a second time; students now fill in all five blanks as they listen. They may adjust answers during a brief pause after the reading ends.

Pairs compare their five answers, noting any differences, then the teacher reads the correct completions aloud and students check. Teacher explains how each answer is drawn from a specific phrase in the transcript.

Brief reflective discussion: teacher asks students whether the podcast's message about meditation and memory connects in any way to the story's meditation on memory and old age — a thematic bridge that is open-ended and voluntary.

periods.teacher_notes: The key precision errors in sentence-completion listening tasks are paraphrasing (writing 'stress reduction' when the transcript says 'stress management') and over-extending (writing four words when three are permitted). Remind students before the second reading to listen for the exact phrasing around each blank's keyword. The thematic connection to Grandpa's memory is not required for the task but gives students a moment to synthesise across the chapter.
materials: Textbook pp.116–117 (Listen and Respond, Task I)

periods.activity_title: Intonation Practice and Personal Caregiving Presentation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Speaking Activity (p.117): intonation in questions — paired practice with story questions, falling and rising patterns
Speaking Activity (p.117–118): brief personal presentation on caring for an older person — structured by four given prompts

homework.task_brief: Writing Task (p.118): article for school magazine — 'Our Inspiring Elderly', four-paragraph structure, title and name required

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces falling and rising intonation using the board examples (Wh-questions fall; Yes/No questions rise; tag questions follow main-clause polarity), then reads two story questions aloud and asks students to echo with correct intonation. Pairs then select two or three questions from the story and practise them together.

Students prepare a short oral presentation (about ninety seconds each) using the four prompts: background of the caregiving experience, what they learned about themselves, understanding the older person's needs, and what insights that gave them about ageing. Teacher circulates during preparation, helping students organise their thinking rather than scripting word for word.

Four to six students deliver their presentations; peers listen and note one specific detail they found memorable. Teacher gives brief, warm feedback after each on clarity and one feature of intonation or register.

Teacher sets the writing homework: the four-paragraph school magazine article 'Our Inspiring Elderly' (p.118), explaining the structure and reminding students to write the title and their name. This is to be completed independently.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have not had a caregiving experience can speak about observing care given to a neighbour or grandparent from a distance — the prompts accommodate this. For the intonation work, focus on the practical distinction between Yes/No and Wh- questions rather than the more complex tag-question patterns; the tag-question material can be revisited in the grammar unit if time allows. The writing task is substantial and benefits from the article's clear four-paragraph scaffold — stress that each paragraph has a specific job.
materials: Textbook pp.117–118 (Speaking Activity Tasks I and II; Writing Task)

periods.activity_title: Beyond the Text — Visual Inference, Photo Slideshow, and 'The Lost Child'

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.119): identify the correct walking-stick image matching Grandpa's brass eagle-head description
Learning Beyond the Text (p.120–125): read 'The Lost Child' by Mulk Raj Anand; discuss theme of family attachment with classmates

homework.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.119): collect memorable family photographs and prepare a digital or physical slideshow with captions

time_bands.activity: Students look at the four walking-stick images (p.119) and identify which one matches the story's description — mahogany stick, brass handle carved as an eagle's head. Teacher uses this as a visual-literacy warm-up: close reading of text produces a precise image, and that image can be verified.

Teacher reads 'The Lost Child' by Mulk Raj Anand (pp.120–125) aloud, pausing at the moment the child realises he is lost — the silence before the panic — to let students absorb the contrast between desire and attachment. Students follow in their textbooks.

Small-group discussion: how does the child's rejection of all the fair's attractions once he is lost change the meaning of each one? Groups share their ideas, and teacher facilitates a comparison with Grandpa's story — in both, something desired (independence, a sweet) is complicated by the fear of losing something more fundamental.

Teacher sets the photograph slideshow as a personal homework project, explaining the three required caption elements: when and where the photograph was taken, who is in it, and why it is memorable. This connects the literary theme of memory and family to students' own lives.

periods.teacher_notes: The photograph slideshow (Task II) is a project students complete in their own time and personal space; it is set as homework rather than a class activity so students have access to their family photographs. 'The Lost Child' by Mulk Raj Anand rewards close attention to the escalating list of rejected desires — the toys, sweets, balloons, and roundabout become more poignant each time they are refused — and this pattern is worth naming in the discussion.
materials: Textbook pp.119–125 (Learning Beyond the Text, Tasks I and III)

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis — Memory, Dignity, and What the Story Teaches

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a single question written on the board: 'Who, by the end of the story, actually needs Vitamin-M?' Students write a private one-sentence answer, then share with a partner — a quick activation of the chapter's central irony before the synthesis proper begins.

Teacher-led literary analysis: drawing on the story's content as a whole, the class maps the three main characters (Grandpa, Vidya, Ravi) onto a board grid — what each character wants, fears, and misunderstands about the other two. Students contribute, and teacher draws connections between character behaviour and the story's themes of autonomy, dignity, selective memory, and quiet love.

Comparative discussion: teacher invites students to set 'Vitamin-M' alongside 'The Lost Child' — both stories turn on the fear of losing a loved one and the gap between what is wanted and what matters most. Students identify one parallel and one contrast, sharing with the class.

Students write a personal closing response — three to four sentences: which moment from the chapter they will remember most, and why it matters beyond the story. Teacher circulates and reads over shoulders without correcting; this is a reflective, not evaluated, piece.

Teacher closes the chapter by reading aloud the final two lines of the story — Grandpa's suggestion that Vidya herself needs Vitamin-M and his wink at Ravi — and leaves students with the question: 'What kind of memory does a person most need in a family?' No answer is required; the question belongs to them.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws on the story's full arc and on 'The Lost Child' by Mulk Raj Anand; it assumes students have encountered both texts, but the comparative discussion works even for a class that only read one of them — the themes of family attachment and the fear of loss are present in the main story alone. The personal closing response is intentionally ungraded; its purpose is reflection, not demonstration, and treating it as such signals to students that literature has a value beyond assessment.
materials: Board or display surface for character grid

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, theme, and authorial craft by close-reading and critically reflecting on a prose narrative.
items.source_context: Grandpa's dignity, selective memory, and the comedy of Ravi's secret surveillance of his grandfather in the city.
items.item_stem:
Read the passage above and answer the questions that follow.

1. What does Grandpa's decision to walk out of the flat with his mahogany stick and yellow cap, despite knowing Ravi's mother has left instructions, reveal about his character?
2. How does the phrase 'leaving Ravi in a dilemma' capture the central tension between Ravi's loyalty to his mother and his sympathy for Grandpa?
3. Identify one way the author uses Grandpa's physical appearance — his stick and cap — to show his attitude toward the city life he resents.
items.visual_stimulus:
From the story (p.102):
“Off he went, twirling his walking stick jauntily, leaving Ravi in a dilemma. His grandfather would feel hurt if he insisted on accompanying him and his mother would be furious if she knew Ravi had let him go out on his own.”

expected_elements: Grandpa's exit shows assertive self-determination and refusal to be infantilised.
The dilemma captures Ravi's impossible position between duty and respect for Grandpa's dignity.
The stick and cap signal Grandpa's confidence and identity, contrasting with Vidya's view of him as frail.
Students should ground each answer in specific textual detail from the passage.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, theme, and authorial craft by close-reading and critically reflecting on a prose narrative.
items.source_context: Grandpa's dignity, selective memory, and the comedy of Ravi's secret surveillance of his grandfather in the city.
items.item_stem: At the end of the story, Grandpa tells Ravi's mother he had 'a quiet morning' and then presents everyone with birthday gifts — including Ravi, who receives The Best Detective Stories. Evaluate what these two acts together reveal about Grandpa's character, and explain how Asha Nehemiah uses them to challenge the reader's initial impression of Grandpa as a person with failing memory. Support your answer with specific evidence from the story.

expected_elements: Grandpa's 'quiet morning' comment is deliberate irony, not forgetfulness — he is entirely aware of what happened.
Remembering everyone's gift (including Ravi's birthday connection) disproves the failing-memory premise.
The detective story gift shows Grandpa knew all along Ravi was following him — sharp and playful.
Students should cite at least two specific details from the story's ending.
A strong response names the theme of selective memory or intergenerational dignity explicitly.

items.source_lo: Student extracts precise information from a spoken informational text by completing sentence-level gaps using exact heard words.
items.source_context: Meditation podcast on relaxation, stress management, self-awareness, and the value of daily practice.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the meditation podcast your teacher reads aloud. As you listen, decide whether each statement below is true or false, and write one phrase from the podcast that supports your verdict.

(1) The podcast says meditation removes all thoughts from the mind permanently.
(2) According to the podcast, meditation improves both physical and emotional well-being.
(3) The podcast recommends meditating only during examination periods.

options.text: According to the podcast, meditation improves both physical and emotional well-being.
The podcast recommends meditating only during examination periods.
The podcast says meditation removes all thoughts from the mind permanently.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) False — the podcast says thoughts that cause stress are removed during meditation, not all thoughts permanently. (2) True — the transcript states meditation results in enhanced well-being 'both physically and emotionally'. (3) False — the podcast says to practise meditation 'on a regular basis' and 'make it your routine', not only during exams.

items.source_lo: Student extracts precise information from a spoken informational text by completing sentence-level gaps using exact heard words.
items.source_context: Meditation podcast on relaxation, stress management, self-awareness, and the value of daily practice.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the meditation podcast again. Answer the following questions in one or two sentences each, using information you heard in the podcast.

1. According to the podcast, what happens to a person's perspective on stressful situations after they meditate?
2. The podcast connects daily meditation practice to examination performance. In your own words, explain the link the podcast makes between meditation and handling exam pressure.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. After meditation, the person feels fresh and gains a new perspective on stressful situations, according to the podcast. 2. The podcast states that practising meditation regularly can help lessen exam-related pressure, allowing students to manage challenges with ease.

items.source_context: Personal experience of caring for an older person — background, learning, and insights into the challenges of ageing.
items.item_stem: Recall a time you helped an elderly person — a grandparent, a neighbour, or someone in your community. Describe the experience in about ninety seconds: who the person was, what you did, and what surprised or moved you during the experience. Use a clear beginning, middle, and end.

expected_elements: The response identifies a specific elderly person and situates the experience clearly.
The student describes a concrete action taken, not a general claim of helpfulness.
A personal reaction or surprise is named, showing reflective engagement.
The account has a discernible beginning, middle, and close.
Intonation is natural and appropriate to a recount genre.

items.source_context: Personal experience of caring for an older person — background, learning, and insights into the challenges of ageing.
items.item_stem: In the story, Vidya makes every decision about Grandpa's safety without asking him what he wants. Do you agree that it is sometimes necessary for families to override an elderly person's wishes 'for their own good'? State your position clearly, give two reasons to support it, and acknowledge one reason someone who disagrees with you might offer.

expected_elements: Student states a clear position at the outset — agree, disagree, or conditional.
Two supporting reasons are offered, each grounded in logic or the story's world.
A counter-argument is genuinely acknowledged, not dismissed without engagement.
The response uses appropriate connectives for argument ('however', 'on the other hand').
Delivery is confident; the student does not merely recount the story but argues a case.

items.source_lo: Student composes a structured, multi-paragraph article for a real-world audience using a functional writing scaffold.
items.source_context: The enduring wisdom of senior citizens in a community — their resilience and the lessons younger people draw from them.
items.item_stem: Write a notice for your school notice board, addressed to all students of Grades VIII–X, inviting them to a community event called 'An Afternoon with Our Elders' — a session where retired teachers, grandparents, and elderly neighbours will share skills, stories, and life lessons. Your notice should include the event name, date, venue, what participants can expect, and a warm closing invitation. Write between 80 and 100 words.

expected_elements: Notice follows the standard format: heading, date/venue, body, issuing authority.
Event purpose is stated clearly and the target audience is addressed appropriately.
At least two specific things participants can expect are mentioned.
Tone is warm and inviting, appropriate for a school community notice.
Word count is within the 80–100 range and language is grammatically controlled.

items.source_context: The enduring wisdom of senior citizens in a community — their resilience and the lessons younger people draw from them.
items.item_stem: Write a letter to the editor of a local newspaper arguing that communities should create more opportunities for elderly residents to contribute their skills and knowledge to younger generations — rather than treating them as people who only need care and protection. Use at least two specific reasons to support your argument and address one objection a reader might raise. Write between 150 and 180 words.

expected_elements: Letter follows formal letter-to-editor format: address, date, salutation, body, closing.
A clear central argument is stated and sustained throughout the letter.
Two specific reasons or examples support the argument (not vague generalisations).
One counter-objection is acknowledged and addressed with a reasoned response.
Register is formal and persuasive; word count is within 150–180 range.

items.item_stem:
The sentences below are in direct speech. Rewrite each one in reported speech, making all necessary changes to tense, pronoun, and time expressions.

1. Ravi's mother said to Ravi, "You must stay at home and look after Grandpa today."
2. Grandpa told Ravi's mother, "I had a quiet morning, but I don't know what Ravi was doing."
3. Ravi said, "I cannot follow Grandpa into the barber's shop without him seeing me."

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Ravi's mother told Ravi that he had to / must stay at home and look after Grandpa that day. 2. Grandpa told Ravi's mother that he had had a quiet morning but that he did not know what Ravi had been doing. 3. Ravi said that he could not follow Grandpa into the barber's shop without him seeing him.

items.source_context: The contrast between suppressed desire and overwhelming attachment in a spring fair — Mulk Raj Anand's 'The Lost Child'.
items.item_stem: In 'The Lost Child' by Mulk Raj Anand, a young child eagerly desires toys, sweets, and fairground rides — yet refuses each of them once he realises he is separated from his parents. Explain in a short paragraph why the child's refusal of all the desired objects after he is lost is more powerful than any direct statement about how much he loves his parents would have been. Use specific details from the story in your answer.

expected_elements: Student identifies the contrast between pre-separation desire and post-separation rejection of those same objects.
The refusal shows that parental presence is more valuable than any material desire — stated through action, not speech.
At least one specific desired object (toy, sweet, balloon, roundabout) is named as evidence.
Student explains why showing rather than telling is more emotionally powerful.
Response connects to the theme of attachment that also runs through the Vitamin-M story, if appropriate.

items.source_lo: Student makes interdisciplinary and cross-textual connections by comparing themes of family attachment across two prose narratives.
items.source_context: The contrast between suppressed desire and overwhelming attachment in a spring fair — Mulk Raj Anand's 'The Lost Child'.
items.item_stem:
Design a small comparative project. Choose ONE of the following and complete it:

(a) Create a two-column comparison chart contrasting how 'Vitamin-M' and 'The Lost Child' each show the fear of losing a loved one — citing one specific scene from each story for every point you make. Include at least three points of comparison.

(b) Write a short critical note (120–150 words) exploring how both stories use a moment of crisis — Grandpa going missing and the child becoming lost — to reveal what characters value most. Refer to specific moments in each text.

expected_elements: For (a): chart has at least three clearly labelled comparison points with a scene cited from each story per point.
For (b): both stories are discussed and the 'crisis as revelation' argument is clearly articulated.
Specific scenes are named — e.g. Ravi's relief on finding Grandpa safe; child rejecting the roundabout after being lost.
The student identifies what each text's characters value most (safety/dignity in Vitamin-M; parental presence in The Lost Child).
Work is organised, evidence-based, and goes beyond plot summary to interpretive comparison.
